summary: Empirically, OpenRouter upstream backends serving the SAME model id differ substantially in tool-calling correctness. Replaying one real captured agent payload (11 messages, 24 tools, reasoning=medium) 12 times per backend against qwen/qwen3.6-27b: Alibaba 12/12 clean, CoreWeave 12/12 clean, Morph 12/12 clean, Chutes 1/12 leaked, Phala 1/12 leaked, SiliconFlow 3/12 leaked. Two open questions this session could not close. (1) Mechanism: quantization does NOT explain it -- CoreWeave is fp8 and clean while Phala is unquantized and leaks -- so the cause is backend-specific template extraction, unconfirmed. (2) Durability: backend rosters and behavior change over time, so the shipped allowlist in scripts/goose-openrouter-route-proxy.py (DEFAULT_ONLY) is a dated snapshot, not a stable fact. Note also that 0/12 leaves a ~22 percent 95-percent upper bound on the true leak rate per backend (~10 percent pooled) -- 'clean' here means 'not observed to leak', not 'proven safe'.
proposed_touch_points: scripts/goose-openrouter-route-proxy.py (DEFAULT_ONLY) -- needs a re-measurement cadence rather than a hardcoded list; consider a `--measure` mode that replays a captured payload N times per backend and reports leak rates, so the allowlist can be regenerated from evidence instead of hand-edited, and so users on other models can derive their own

The same OpenRouter model id served by different upstreams differs in fidelity (Alibaba 12/12 and CoreWeave 12/12 clean, Morph degraded); nothing in agentteams/ can change a third party's backend. The measurement is retained in this row's summary as the reason, per the plan at tmp/by-week/2026-W31/cluster-plans-round-2.plan.md.

summary: agentteams/research/search.py::web_search could not distinguish 'the search endpoint blocked us' from 'nothing matched' -- both returned []. Root cause: DuckDuckGo answers a challenged request with HTTP 202 plus an interstitial anomaly/challenge page rather than an error status, so resp.raise_for_status() never fires (202 IS a success code); the challenge page simply yields no regex matches. Measured deterministic 2026-07-24: a long specific query returned 202 with zero results on 4/4 attempts while a shortened form of the same query returned 200 with 10 results. Observed live: an agent that had correctly adopted the tool received [] and was on track to conclude the information did not exist. Fixed by adding _broaden + web_search_verbose (retry once with a broadened query; return a note explaining the fallback or the block) with the CLI printing the note to stderr so stdout JSON stays parseable.
proposed_touch_points: agentteams/research/search.py -- the broadening heuristic (keep the first 4 terms) is a single fixed strategy chosen from one day's observations; consider measuring challenge behavior across query shapes before treating it as general, and consider whether other endpoints (or a fallback engine) should back it up. Also worth auditing other callers of web_search (reputable.py, news.py) that still consume the plain list and therefore cannot see the note
resolved_evidence: _DDG_CHALLENGE_STATUS discrimination plus web_search_verbose's note; tests/test_research_search.py.

summary: memory_index.query_index returns byte-identical documents as separate results. references/bridges/<pair>/agent-inventory.md is the same 8,999-byte file in all three bridge directories (identical sha256), and a query matching it fills all three top-3 slots with one document's content. Found 2026-07-31 when tests/test_memory_index_relevance.py::test_top3_accuracy_perfect went red: the three copies tied at 8.7782 and pushed the genuinely correct answer to fourth at 8.7777, a 0.006% gap opened by unrelated prose added elsewhere in references/ shifting BM25 background statistics. Relevance did not regress -- the benchmark was knife-edge because duplicates occupied the slots. The BENCHMARK was fixed by deduplicating its corpus on content hash; the product was left alone deliberately, because whether a retrieval API should collapse identical results for real callers (and which path it should then report) is a design question, not a bug fix.
proposed_touch_points: agentteams/memory_index.py::query_index -- consider collapsing results whose content hash matches, reporting one path plus a duplicate count; OR leave as-is and document that callers may receive duplicates. Either way the k= contract should say which. Note the same shape would affect --query-index and /recall output, not just the test.
resolved_evidence: DECIDED 2026-08-06: do not collapse. A collapsed hit must report ONE path and which path is right depends on the caller — an agent resolving a reference wants its own bridge directory, an auditor counting exposure wants all three; picking silently is wrong for one of them with no way to tell which. The decision is now IMPLEMENTED as contract rather than left implicit: agentteams/memory_index.py::query_index documents that hits may contain byte-identical documents, states why collapsing was rejected, and points callers at content-hash de-duplication at their own layer. Not a defect — by design.

summary: tests/test_memory_index_performance.py::test_build_index_scaling_is_reasonable is a WALL-CLOCK assertion and it flakes in CI. The assertion compares a 120-document build against 4x a 60-document build plus a 50ms floor, and the 60-doc baseline measured 3.3ms -- so the multiplicative term contributes ~13ms and the whole test rests on a 50ms absolute budget on a shared runner. Both measurements are trivially fast; nothing is actually slow. summary: --dry-run under-reports a CAPABILITY GRANT change. Rehearsing the claude-team merge showed 12 changed files where --dry-run predicted 7. Four of the extras are build artifacts (build-log.json, delivery-receipt.json, memory-index.json/.vcache) and are uninteresting. The fifth is not: reference-manager.md, which --dry-run reports as UNCHANGED while the real run widens its allowed-tools from 'Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob' to include 'Bash(python -m agentteams.research:*)'. NOT AN ENGINE DEFECT -- verified by calling _merge_front_matter directly: with no build-log baseline the deployed grant is KEPT and drift is reported ('Kept yours; reconcile by hand'); with a baseline proving the file is unmodified since generation the template value is applied AND a notice is emitted ("front matter: 'allowed-tools' updated to ... (unmodified since generation)"). The grant comes from the template's own tools:['read','edit','search','retrieval'] and the retrieval token maps to that Bash entry, so it is intended and provenance-gated. The defect is that the PREVIEW does not show it: the real run emits the notice, --dry-run emits nothing and says UNCHANGED. A capability widening is exactly the change C-3 makes privileged, and --dry-run is what an operator uses to decide whether to proceed. Found only because the merge was rehearsed against an isolated copy of the tree rather than trusted from its dry run.
proposed_touch_points: --dry-run should run the same front-matter merge and surface its notices, and should not classify a file as UNCHANGED when only its front matter changes; the file-level verb is computed from body content alone

summary: A brief edit that changes only PLACEHOLDER VALUES does not propagate to fenced regions on --update --merge. Found while remediating audit finding D-7: .github/agents/_build-description.json had three fields naming paths that do not exist (primary_output_dir 'src/', figures_dir 'docs/figures/', reference_db_path null while the rendered table named docs/ as the reference DB). After correcting all three, `build_team.py --self --update --merge` reported 'No structural or template-content changes detected' and left the directory_structure fence showing the old values. This is NOT a stale-manifest artifact: analyze.build_manifest re-read from disk and resolved the new values correctly (verified directly), so the loss is downstream of analyze, in the drift/merge decision.
